cells.tense: You've got hold of one line right now and you're keeping it, and the keeping isn't costing you much.
cells.ask: Tell the person who's in this with you what's keeping the line steady, and let them add what they see — you get a shared weight back, not a handed-off decision.
cells.core:
There's a clean version of this and you're in it: one direction chosen, held while it gets tested, and you staying level while you do. The grip is on the thing you chose, not on winning it. It reads as steady because it is.

Where a line like this is free to go next is into a second set of hands. You've been the one carrying it, and no one's had a piece of it alongside you. Letting someone already in this take a share isn't a step down. Held alone over a long season, a line tends to starve for exactly the thing it can't give itself.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding one line, and keeping it isn't costing you.
cells.verb: gathering what's scattered into one direction and holding it where it meets push
cells.place: the spot where each side gets its due and what's out of proportion is being set right

cells.tense: You're standing in a fight that hasn't arrived, and every move gets made before the one that actually comes.
cells.ask: Leave the argument alone for one day, and write down what has to be true before you'd let the other person have any of it.
cells.core:
Held well, this looks like a direction chosen and kept through pushback that actually lands. No rehearsal needed — the grip is there when it's tested because it's on the line, not on the contest about the line.

Your days have gone the other way. The rehearsal runs first and runs long, and a good share of what you're braced against is a fight you've scripted rather than one that's come. Bracing costs the same as holding and spends it on nothing that's arrived. Leave the argument untouched for a day. Put one line on paper about what has to hold before you'd give an inch. You'll see whether the grip is still on the direction you chose or has slid onto the argument about it — and both answers are usable.
cells.sheetLine: You're braced for a fight that hasn't started and that somebody else may never bring.

cells.tense: The direction got picked up a while back and then set down, and yesterday's next step is what's still in front of you.
cells.ask: Write down one thing that's actually uneven right now, and what would have to be true before you'd call it settled — one line, today.
cells.core:
A direction taken up and kept doesn't have to be loud to be real. It's held quietly, and it's still there when the load comes. That's the shape you're after.

What happens instead is the grip lets go without a decision to let it go. The step after the hard part doesn't get taken, and the line that would have made the step decided slides off the table. Nobody chose to drop it; the picking back up just didn't happen. Two things on paper — what's out of proportion, and what would have to be true before you'd call it settled — put one thing back on the table it came off of. That's what a dropped hold waits for.

cells.tense: You're living inside the grip and telling it as if it costs you nothing — the days are already shaped by what you're keeping.
cells.ask: Take one line you've already kept and say out loud, in your own words, that you're the one who held it.
cells.core:
Working well, the grip is visible to the person doing the gripping — you know which lines are yours, and you can say so without making a case out of it. The grip and the naming run together.

Yours runs without the naming. You keep some things even when nobody asked, in how you spend your days and what you stay late for, and the story around that is that it costs nothing or that it's just how things are. The line is real. The fact that you're the one keeping it has gone unclaimed. One line you've already kept, said out loud as yours — not a boast, just the record catching up to what your days already show.

attempts.check: The draft's weakest claim is that the person is personally defending something against resistance — the card says the capacity gathers and holds when direction is chosen, not that the person has picked a fight. A reader might say the friction where they stand isn't opposition from anyone, just drift, and No. 7's harvest language is my gloss not their report. The asks survive being wrong: writing down what has to be true before a thing is settled, leaving the argument alone for a day, writing down one fact of the split instead of arguing it, and keeping the record of a fix tell the person something either way. The sentence that serves me too much is the fight framing; I'm narrowing it to grip on a direction and its cost, not a stance on other people.
